title: Citizen Kane
objective: After this level you can explain why Citizen Kane's deep focus, low angles and jumbled timeline made it a film that filmmakers study.
summary: Citizen Kane (1941) used Gregg Toland's deep focus, low angles under muslin ceilings, and flashbacks from five witnesses; a box-office disappointment, it became one of the most influential films.

cards.headline: A 1941 box-office disappointment became the film filmmakers study.
cards.body: Orson Welles made Citizen Kane at RKO when he was 25, directing, co-writing it with Herman Mankiewicz and playing the lead. Critics praised it, ticket sales disappointed, and it won a single Oscar, for its screenplay. Three choices turned it into a textbook: what's sharp, where the camera sits and when things happen.

cards.headline: Everything in focus
cards.body: Cinematographer Gregg Toland wanted the whole frame sharp, near and far. With faster Eastman film, wide-angle lenses set to small openings and powerful arc lamps, he reached a depth of field close to your own eye's. In nearly every scene, faces and objects are sharp in all parts of the screen, so the film lets you choose where to look.

mascot.line: Don't memorize the lens recipe. Remember the result: near and far, all sharp, and you pick where to look.

cards.headline: Looking up at Kane
cards.body: Welles and Toland often set the camera low and shot upward. That meant trouble: Hollywood sets usually had no ceilings, because the lights hung from the rafters. So Toland had ceilings made of muslin cloth, which also let microphones hide just above them. In 1941, those low-angled shots that revealed ceilings looked powerful and modern.

cards.headline: A life in pieces
cards.body: The film opens with Kane's death. A reporter then questions people who knew him, and the story unfolds in flashbacks: the shifting, not always reliable accounts of five former intimates. Welles called it prismatic. You assemble Kane yourself, like a detective with clashing witnesses. It's one reason Citizen Kane became one of the most influential films ever made.

learned: Toland's deep focus: near and far, all sharp

questions.prompt: Who was the cinematographer behind Citizen Kane's deep focus?

options.label: Joseph Breen
options.rationale: Breen ran the Production Code office.

questions.explanation: Gregg Toland used fast film, wide-angle lenses and arc lamps to keep near and far sharp.

questions.prompt: Why did Citizen Kane's sets need ceilings when most Hollywood sets had none?

options.label: The Production Code required closed rooms
options.rationale: The code dealt with content, not set design.

options.label: Low camera angles looked up, where a ceiling would show
Technicolor cameras needed a roof to bounce light
options.rationale: Citizen Kane was shot in black and white.

options.label: RKO filmed on outdoor lots in the rain
options.rationale: It was shot on sets, with lights usually in the rafters.

questions.explanation: Shooting upward from low angles would have revealed the empty rafters, so Toland built muslin ceilings.

questions.prompt: Level 41's early talkies kept actors near short-range microphones. How did Kane's muslin ceilings help with sound?

options.label: The cloth amplified the actors' voices
options.rationale: It hid the microphones; it didn't amplify anything.

options.label: They blocked noise from the camera
options.rationale: Camera noise was handled by housings, not ceilings.

options.label: They reflected sound back to the audience
options.rationale: The ceilings were on the set, not in theaters.

options.label: Microphones could hide just above them

questions.explanation: Muslin ceilings let microphones sit just overhead and out of sight, even in shots that looked up.
